title: Quicksort, stability and .NET's sort
summary: Partition around a pivot, see why stability matters, and know when Array.Sort is all you need.

steps.title: Partition around a pivot
body: **Quicksort** picks a **pivot** value and **partitions** the array: everything smaller than the pivot moves to its left, everything else to its right. The pivot is then in its final place, and each side is sorted the same way.

This is the **Lomuto** partition, with the last item as pivot. `store` marks where the next small value goes. Each time `a[j]` is smaller than the pivot it is swapped down to `store`. At the end the pivot is swapped into `store`.
Watch the small values gather on the left. The pivot `5` lands at index 3.

steps.explain: 1 and 3 are smaller than the pivot 5, so they are swapped to slots 0 and 1. The pivot then swaps into slot 2. Here the array happens to come out sorted; usually only the pivot is final.

steps.title: Quicksort and its worst case
body: void QuickSort(int[] a, int lo, int hi)
When the pivot splits the range roughly in half, there are `log n` levels of `O(n)` work: **O(n log n)**, and in practice quicksort is very fast because it sorts in place.

But with last-item pivots, an **already sorted** array is the worst case: every pivot is the largest, one side is empty, and the work becomes **O(n²)**. Real implementations pick a better pivot (the middle item, or the median of three) to avoid it.

steps.prompt: Quicksort with last-item pivots is given `1, 2, 3, ..., 10000`. What happens?
options: Every partition peels off only one item, so it does about n²/2 comparisons
It finishes instantly because the data is sorted
It does about n log n comparisons, as usual
It throws, because the pivot is the maximum
steps.explain: Each pivot is the biggest value in its range, so the 'smaller' side holds everything else. The recursion is also `n` levels deep, which can overflow the stack.

steps.title: Stability
body: A sort is **stable** if items that compare equal keep their original order.
It matters when you sort by one key after another: sort orders by time, then stably by customer, and each customer's orders stay in time order.
| insertion sort, merge sort, bubble sort | selection sort, quicksort, heap sort |
`Array.Sort` is an *introsort*: quicksort that switches to heap sort if it goes badly and to insertion sort for small pieces. Fast, in place, and not stable.

steps.prompt: `OrderBy` is stable. What does this print?
steps.explain: Bo and Di both score 1 and keep their original order; so do Ann and Cy with 3.
Selection sort's long-distance swap can jump an item over an equal one. Quicksort's partition does the same.

steps.prompt: In everyday C#, when should you write your own sort?
options: Almost never: use `Array.Sort`, `List.Sort` or `OrderBy` with a key or comparer
Whenever the data has more than 1,000 items
Whenever you need a stable sort
Always, because the built-in sorts are O(n²)
steps.explain: The built-in sorts are `O(n log n)` and heavily tuned. Need stability? Use `OrderBy`. You write sorts to *understand* them, and for the rare special case (merging huge files, counting sort on tiny ranges).
